accroche: Hume is credited with a law forbidding the derivation of a value from a fact. His 1740 text does not quite say that.
contenu_vulgarise:
A philosophy textbook often lays down, as a stable axiom, the idea that one can never derive an ought from an is. The authority invoked is almost always the same: David Hume, and what has since been called his “guillotine,” as if he had settled the question once and for all, in 1740, in his *A Treatise of Human Nature*.

## What the Text Really Says

The passage does exist. It closes a chapter in which Hume has just shown, in his own way, that reason alone never discovers good and evil. He then notices something that surprises him: in almost all the systems of morality he knows, the author reasons at first in the ordinary way (proving the existence of God, or describing human affairs), then suddenly shifts to propositions tied to an *ought* or an *ought not*, without ever explaining the transition. He writes, in the English of the Treatise: “I meet with no proposition that is not connected with an ought, or an ought not.”

What Hume asks for at this moment is not a prohibition. It is an explanation. He adds that this new relation should be observed and explained, and that such attention would be enough, by itself, to overturn the ordinary systems of morality he knows. The text is a demand addressed to the moralists of his time, not a logical law stated for eternity.

## The Shift

The general law taught today under the name “Hume's guillotine,” or more soberly “Hume's law,” comes from elsewhere. The label itself is a twentieth-century construction: it is associated with an article by the philosopher Max Black published in 1964, and authors such as R. M. Hare then installed the expression “Hume's Law” in the everyday vocabulary of Anglo-American metaethics. Neither is Hume's: he never named his observation, much less formulated a law under that name.

Scholars of the Treatise disagree among themselves about the exact scope of the passage. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy lists several competing readings, without deciding between them: a general reading, dominant since the twentieth century, that makes it a universal logical principle forbidding any evaluative conclusion from factual premises; a narrower reading, which limits the point to the initial discovery of the ideas of vice and virtue, which requires sentiment rather than reason alone. Neither imposes itself on a reading of the text.

What the 1740 paragraph asked was that one be owed an explanation. Nearly two and a half centuries later, among readers of the Treatise, the discussion still owes it.

carte.punch: “Hume's guillotine” is a twentieth-century name, not a formula from the 1740 Treatise.
carte.idee: Hume does not decree that one can never derive an ought from an is: he asks that this transition be explained, and adds that such attention would be enough to overturn common morality. The name “Hume's guillotine” dates from a 1964 article, two centuries later.

quiz.question: What exactly does Hume ask for in the paragraph often called the “guillotine”?
choix: That all moral conclusions be abandoned, reason having no part in good and evil
That the transition from is to ought be explained, which he judges almost always left unjustified
That the notion of moral duty be replaced by that of social utility, which is more measurable
That natural good be distinguished from moral good, to avoid the error Moore would later denounce
quiz.explication: Hume lays down no logical prohibition: he asks that the transition from is to ought be observed and explained, and adds that such attention would be enough to overturn the ordinary systems of morality. The other three propositions describe distinct debates, some of them well after his 1740 text.
